claims.text: The target material initially contains a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution.
Controlled thermal aging at 300–600 °C initiates diffusion and intermetallic formation in Mg-containing lightweight HEAs.
Thermal activation causes Mg atoms to segregate.
Segregated Mg nucleates and grows fine-scale Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates form preferentially at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Mg-containing lightweight HEAs have a tendency to contain or develop complex precipitate phases.
A limited volume fraction of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates locally modifies surface chemistry and stabilizes a protective oxide layer.
Excessive intermetallic formation depletes key elements from the metastable matrix.
Elemental depletion promotes the formation of non-protective oxide scales.
Non-protective oxide formation diminishes corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The transformation kinetics and intermetallic volume fraction determine whether protective surface properties are retained or lost.
Samples with minor precipitation after aging will retain an adherent protective oxide and good corrosion and oxidation resistance.
Samples with extensive Mg-rich intermetallic precipitation will have poorer oxide-film integrity and corrosion performance than the as-cast state.
The as-cast comparison state has minimal intermetallic formation.
The proposed mechanism operates from 300–600 °C under chloride exposure, provided complete phase transformation or melting does not occur.
A controlled comparison between identically prepared thermally aged samples and as-cast samples can test the proposed mechanism.
Absence of a statistically significant association between Mg-rich intermetallic precipitation and changes in oxide quality and corrosion or oxidation resistance would refute the hypothesis.
